subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: First, you learn that data helps us solve problems — we collect the data, look at it carefully, understand what it tells us, and then make a good decision. Third, you learn to organise and present data as a tally chart, a pictogram, and a block or column chart, and to read a chart to answer questions. Fourth, you learn how data is recorded on computers using input devices and electronic forms, and you make one simple chart on screen.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Understand that data helps us solve problems, using the steps collect the data, look at it, understand it, and then decide.
Tell the difference between categorical data (groups and words) and discrete data (whole numbers).
Collect and organise data using a tally chart and a table.
Present data as a pictogram and a block or column chart, and recognise a bar chart and a pie chart.
Read a chart and answer questions about it (most, least, how many more, how many altogether).
Choose the right input device (keyboard or a pointing device) to record discrete or categorical data on an electronic form.
Make a simple column chart on the computer using a free spreadsheet.

toolkit.name: A free spreadsheet
steps: Open a new blank spreadsheet.
Put your field names in row 1, one per column.
Type one record per row underneath.
Use Insert → Chart to turn your data into a graph.
toolkit.note: Any free spreadsheet works — the ideas are the same in all of them.

concepts.title: Data helps us solve problems
concepts.explanation:
Data is the facts and numbers we collect. Data helps us solve problems and make good choices. There are three steps: first we collect the data, then we look at it carefully, then we understand what it is telling us. After that, we can make a good decision.

When we want to solve a problem, we do not just guess. We collect some facts — that is data. Then we look at the data and think about what it means.
concepts.example: Then we can decide what to do. Let us try it.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you see that data helps us decide, instead of guessing? Can you count carefully and make neat tally marks?

concepts.title: Two kinds of data: categorical and discrete
concepts.explanation:
There are two kinds of data. Categorical data sorts things into groups, and is usually words — like favourite fruit (mango, banana, dates) or the colour of a car.

Some data is words that put things in groups — we call that categorical. Some data is numbers we count — we call that discrete.
concepts.example: Discrete numbers are always whole. You cannot have two and a half children in a class, or half a brother!
concepts.checkYourself: Can you remember that discrete numbers are whole? A common slip is to call a favourite thing a number — gently show you that mango is a group, and the 5 is the count. Can you tell a group (words) from a count (numbers)?

concepts.title: Showing data: tallies, pictograms and charts
concepts.explanation:
Once we have collected data, we make it easy to read by showing it as a picture. First we count with a tally chart (marks in groups of five). Then we can show the same data as a pictogram (pictures with a key), a block graph or column chart (blocks or columns standing up — taller means more), or a bar chart (bars lying down — longer means more). A pie chart is a circle cut into slices — a bigger slice means more.

Which is your favourite — milk, juice or water? For example Start with a class vote you can see. Remind you how tally marks work: one line for each, and every fifth mark makes a group of five, so they are easy to count.
concepts.example: Find one real example of showing data: tallies, pictograms and charts around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: When you colour the block graph, Can you colour the right number of blocks? Can you use the key on a pictogram (not just count dots blindly)?

concepts.title: Making a chart on the computer
concepts.explanation:
Computers can make charts for us quickly. We put our data into a spreadsheet as a table, select it, and ask the computer to draw the chart. We will use LibreOffice Calc, which is free.

A box has a name from its letter and number, like A1. We type our data into the boxes, then the computer draws the chart for us.
concepts.example: Open LibreOffice Calc on the projector. Explain in child words that a spreadsheet is a big grid of boxes (cells), with letters across the top (A, B) and numbers down the side (1, 2, 3).
concepts.checkYourself: Can you select the data and find Insert then Chart? Can you type each piece of data into the correct box? Do not worry about neat formatting — making the chart at all is the success.

concepts.title: Collecting data with computing devices
concepts.explanation:
Data can be collected straight into a computer using an electronic form (a form you fill in on a screen). We put data in using input devices. A keyboard is best for typing numbers and words. A pointing device — a mouse, touchpad or touchscreen — is best for clicking or ticking a box. The type of question tells us which device to use.

Look at question one. It asks you to tick a box to choose a fruit. To tick a box, what do you use — a keyboard, or a mouse or touchscreen? Now look at question two.
concepts.example: It asks how many bananas you want. To type a number, what do you use?
concepts.checkYourself: This session ties the whole unit together — data, kinds of data, and how we record it. Can you match a tick-box question to a pointing device, and a number question to the keyboard?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: (a) a pointing device (mouse, touchpad or touchscreen); (b) categorical data.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in making a chart on the computer, and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Computers can make charts for us quickly. We put our data into a spreadsheet as a table, select it, and ask the computer to draw the chart. We will use LibreOffice Calc, which is free.

A box has a name from its letter and number, like A1. We type our data into the boxes, then the computer draws the chart for us.

project.title: Unit 3 Project: Be a Data Expert
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Data Expert into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a data expert project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I asked 10 children and made a tally mark for each answer.
I counted the tally marks and wrote the numbers.
I showed my data as a pictogram (one picture for each child).
I said which fruit is the most popular and which is the least.

selfAssessment: I can understand that data helps us solve problems, using the steps collect the data, look at it, understand it, and then decide.
I can tell the difference between categorical data (groups and words) and discrete data (whole numbers).
I can collect and organise data using a tally chart and a table.
I can present data as a pictogram and a block or column chart, and recognise a bar chart and a pie chart.
I can read a chart and answer questions about it (most, least, how many more, how many altogether).
I can choose the right input device (keyboard or a pointing device) to record discrete or categorical data on an electronic form.
I can make a simple column chart on the computer using a free spreadsheet.
